title: The Thing About Minds (with Help from Toni Morrison)
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart builds this depressurization-series entry around Dallas Willard's claim that our basic freedom lies in where we put our mind, arguing that most teachers default into unexamined rumination — 'I'm so bad at this job,' 'these students are so mean' — without noticing whether that rumination helps or harms them. He anchors the piece in Toni Morrison's New Yorker essay describing how her father reframed a miserable adolescent job with a few short sentences, distilling four durable thoughts she carried the rest of her life: do the work well for yourself, the job doesn't define you, your real life is with your people, and you are not your work. Stuart is careful to note that intentional contemplation isn't magical thinking that replaces necessary action, but argues it's radically undervalued in an age of cheap expression and plentiful outrage. He closes with concrete mechanisms — writing a chosen thought on an index card and placing it somewhere visible, reading five minutes of non-teaching material daily, and taking contemplative walks — for actually practicing deliberate contemplation rather than just endorsing it in the abstract.
points: Stuart's organizing claim, borrowed from Dallas Willard, is that 'our choice as to where we put our mind is what most determines where we go' — reframing contemplation as an act of agency rather than passive mood.

He names the default failure mode explicitly: most people 'meditate on default,' ruminating at length on spontaneous or externally-presented thoughts without ever asking whether that rumination helps or harms them.

The Toni Morrison anecdote supplies four transferable, memorized thoughts (you are not your job; the job doesn't make you; your real life is with your people; do the work well for yourself) as a model of what deliberately chosen contemplation can look like in practice.

He explicitly guards against the piece being read as pure mindset magic, conceding 'we're not brains on sticks' and that many circumstances require real action — while still arguing intentional contemplation is underrated.
His practical mechanisms (index cards with chosen thoughts, five minutes of non-teaching reading daily, contemplative walks) turn an abstract philosophical claim into a repeatable daily habit.
quotes: It isn't too much of an exaggeration to say that our basic freedom is where we put our mind. It's not unlimited; we can be captured by our thoughts. But our choice as to where we put our mind is what most determines where we go.
The thing is, most of us meditate on default. We look thoughtfully at length at thoughts that others present to us, or that occur to us spontaneously.
Listen. You don't live there. You live here. With your people. Go to work. Get your money. And come on home.
I have never considered the level of labor to be the measure of myself, and I have never placed the security of a job above the value of home.
It goes without saying, but just to be sure: you can't change reality just by thinking nice thoughts. We're not brains on sticks. Many circumstances require action and voice.
But in an age where expression is cheap and outrage is plentiful, intentional contemplation is radically under-rated.
